Thomas Stonewall Jackson. A Confederate general of the American Civil War, renowned for his aggressive tactics and rapid movements. Jackson acquired his famous nickname at the First Battle of Bull Run in eighteen sixty-one, where his steadfast defensive position inspired Confederate confidence and became emblematic of his later reputation.

He demonstrated his tactical brilliance during the Shenandoah Valley campaigns in the spring of eighteen sixty-two. Using rapid marches, terrain knowledge, and surprise attacks, Jackson defeated three larger Union armies without being decisively defeated himself. He was one of the Confederacy's few accomplished offensive strategists, and his aggressive doctrines and lightning movements contrasted sharply with the more cautious Confederate generals.

Jackson became Robert E. Lee's right arm, trusted above all other commanders. Lee famously said after Jackson's wounding: I have lost my right arm. Later, when Jackson died, Lee would say: I have lost my left arm. Throughout his military career, Jackson maintained deep religious devotion, viewing himself as an instrument of Providence, leading to pious personal behavior and deep Christian conviction.

During the Battle of Chancellorsville, Jackson was shot accidentally by his own troops while conducting a night reconnaissance. He died nine days later in May of eighteen sixty-three. His death marked a turning point in Confederate fortunes, removing the general Lee deemed most essential to Southern victory and weakening Confederate command structure at a critical moment. Jackson shares a close military bond with Robert E. Lee, whose army he served as an indispensable partner.
